questions.html: How many ways can 6 different diplomats be assigned to 5 different continents?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

We have:

  • 6 distinct diplomats (label them D1, D2, …, D6)
  • 5 distinct continents (label them C1, C2, …, C5)
  • We want to assign each diplomat to a continent.
  • Each diplomat must be assigned to exactly one continent, but a continent can have multiple diplomats.

This is a classic assignment or distribution problem.

For each diplomat, we can choose any of the 5 continents to assign them to. So this is a case of repetition allowed, and order matters (since the diplomats are distinct).

This is not a permutation or combination in the usual "choose k from n" sense — rather, it’s a mapping from the set of diplomats to continents.

So, for:

  • Diplomat 1 → 5 choices
  • Diplomat 2 → 5 choices
  • ...
  • Diplomat 6 → 5 choices

Using the multiplication principle, we get:

5 × 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 56 = 15,625

 Why not use permutations?

Permutations apply when you're arranging or selecting distinct items without repetition — for example:

  • Assigning 5 of the 6 diplomats to 5 continents, with only one diplomat per continent — then you'd use permutations:

P(6, 5) = 6! / (6 − 5)! = 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 720

But in your case, multiple diplomats can go to the same continent — there's no restriction that each continent gets only one diplomat.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Here the diplomats are unique and so are the continents so it is a DODB problem. Think of this as lining up the 6 diplomats and labelling each with one of 5 continents - this is really just $5^6$. Or think of this as simply permutation with repetition (not repeated items). 6 spaces, 5 options each.

  • By using IODB Template ,stars bars concept.

  • Boxes won't have zero,  because if 0 is selected firstly it cannot be n digit and secondly later on other digits we cannot select 0 because of non decreasing order of the digits( should be increasing order)

questions.html: How many 7 digit decreasing numbers are there? One example is 9777650 .
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

This is the number of ways to choose 7 digits out of 10 total with repetition. There are $\binom{7+10-1}{10-1}=\binom{16}{9}$ ways to do this. But, if we choose all 0's, then this is not a 7 digit number so we have to get rid of that case and that is the only bad case. So, there are a total of $\binom{16}{9}-1$ total ways.
